Free AQA GCSE Geography Introduction Lesson

Blog > 2026 > Free AQA GCSE Geography Introduction Lesson

  • Click to share
  • Click to share

Free AQA GCSE Geography Introduction Lesson

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:15
Instaread

Starting a new GCSE Geography course is an opportunity to do more than introduce students to a specification. It is a chance to show them what studying Geography at GCSE is actually about: exploring real events, asking geographical questions, making connections and understanding an increasingly complex world.

Our new Introduction to AQA GCSE Geography lesson has been designed as an engaging first lesson for students beginning the course. Rather than treating the different areas of the specification as completely separate topics, the lesson introduces students to one of the most important ideas in Geography from the outset: everything is connected.

The PowerPoint is accompanied by a downloadable Geography in the News article and includes teacher notes with practical suggestions for delivering the activities, supporting literacy and providing appropriate support and challenge.

Start with the big picture

The lesson provides students with a clear overview of the structure of the AQA GCSE Geography course, including the three examination papers and the main areas of study.

Students are introduced to:

  • Paper 1 – Living with the Physical Environment: The Challenge of Natural Hazards, The Living World and Physical Landscapes in the UK.
  • Paper 2 – Challenges in the Human Environment: Urban Issues and Challenges, The Changing Economic World and The Challenge of Resource Management.
  • Paper 3 – Geographical Applications: Issue Evaluation and fieldwork.

This gives students an early understanding of the course they are about to begin without turning the lesson into a lengthy tour of the specification.

Geography in the News

The next stage brings the course to life through real geographical events from summer 2026.

Students encounter seven stories from the UK and around the world, including:

  • heatwaves and drought in the UK
  • falling rates of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest
  • the major earthquake in Indonesia
  • the catastrophic glacier collapse and flooding in Nepal
  • the demolition of homes in Makoko, Lagos
  • rapid coastal erosion on the Holderness Coast
  • changes to car manufacturing at Nissan’s Sunderland factory.

The stories have deliberately been selected to cover a broad range of physical and human geography.

Students are challenged to match each news story to an area of the AQA GCSE Geography course.

This provides a simple way of checking their existing geographical understanding while demonstrating that the topics they are about to study aren’t abstract ideas confined to a textbook – they are happening around them now.

Everything is connected…

Having encouraged students to place the news stories across different areas of the specification, the lesson then challenges the idea that Geography can be divided so neatly.

A familiar chocolate bar is used to demonstrate how something seemingly simple can be connected to climate, ecosystems, resources, farming, manufacturing, trade, urbanisation and economic development.

The central message is:

Geography explores how people and places are connected.

This provides an accessible introduction to synoptic thinking before students are asked to apply it to a much more complex geographical event.

From a chocolate bar to a real geographical event

Students then receive the accompanying newspaper-style Geography in the News article:

Britain’s Summer of Extremes: Heatwaves and Drought Put the Country Under Pressure
The article explores the exceptionally hot and dry summer of 2026 and deliberately provides students with opportunities to discover connections for themselves.

It considers the impacts of heat and drought on river flows, reservoirs, ecosystems, wildlife, agriculture, food production, water supplies, businesses, infrastructure and communities, as well as responses to the challenges created by a warmer climate.

The important point is that the article doesn’t tell students which GCSE unit each section relates to.

That’s their job.

Working in pairs, students identify as many connections as possible between the geographical event and the different areas of the GCSE course.

Rather than accepting a simple connection such as “Living World – wildlife”, students can be encouraged to develop their thinking using:

Article evidence → geographical connection → explanation

This moves the activity beyond simply spotting topics and towards explaining why geographical processes, places and people are connected.

Literacy is built into the activity

The article also provides an opportunity to develop disciplinary literacy alongside geographical understanding.

There are detailed teacher notes in the PowerPoint, so make sure you review them before teaching the lesson. They contain practical suggestions for adapting and delivering the activity with your class.

Suggested approaches include a first read for gist, followed by a second reading in which students identify causes, effects and responses.

Students can also identify and explore important geographical vocabulary, including drought, precipitation, discharge, drainage basin, reservoir, irrigation, groundwater, evaporation, transpiration, infrastructure, and adaptation.

Quick retrieval questions can then be used to check that students have understood the article before asking them to tackle the more demanding synoptic task.

The teacher notes also include ideas for support and challenge, including ways to scaffold connections for students who need additional help and to extend more confident students by asking them to identify connections among the different consequences they have identified.

The journey through GCSE Geography

Once students have begun to understand what GCSE Geography involves, the lesson looks ahead.

A visual Our Journey roadmap introduces the sequence of major course components, from Natural Hazards and The Living World through physical and human geography to fieldwork and Issue Evaluation.

This gives students a visual overview of where their GCSE Geography journey will take them and can be adapted by departments to reflect their own curriculum sequence.

What skills will students develop?

GCSE Geography isn’t simply about acquiring more geographical knowledge.

The lesson introduces students to some of the skills they will develop throughout the course, including:

Data analysis | Problem solving | Map skills | Fieldwork | Communication | Critical thinking

Students are shown how these involve interpreting maps, graphs and statistics; applying knowledge to unfamiliar situations; evaluating evidence; collecting and using geographical data; and communicating ideas using accurate geographical vocabulary.

These are skills they will repeatedly return to throughout their GCSE course.

Finish with reflection

The lesson concludes with a short exit reflection:

What have you discovered about GCSE Geography that you didn’t know at the start of the lesson?

Students can use three prompts to structure their thinking:

  • What will we study?
  • How are the topics connected?
  • Why might Geography help us make sense of the world and shape the future?

It provides a simple way to return to the lesson’s purpose and to check whether students’ understanding of GCSE Geography has developed.

What’s included?

The download includes the editable PowerPoint lesson, the accompanying newspaper-style Geography in the News article and detailed teacher notes within the presentation.

The notes are worth exploring before delivering the lesson. They contain additional guidance and ideas not included on the student-facing slides, particularly for the reading and synoptic activities.

The resource has been designed so departments can use it as provided or edit it to reflect their own curriculum journey and approach.

Most importantly, the lesson aims to establish an important idea from the beginning of GCSE Geography:

The course may be divided into different topics, but the world isn’t. Geography helps us understand the connections between them.
